## Agenda

1. Why invest in education?
2. Two theories of the wage return
3. The causal problem
4. Difference-in-differences
5. Duflo (2001)

## Deadlines

# Why Education?

## The Big Claim

::: incremental
- Education is often called the highest-return investment in development
- Girls' schooling has been linked to lower fertility, lower child mortality, higher incomes
- Cross-country: years of schooling correlates strongly with GDP per capita
- Is this causal, or is it the selection story all over again?
:::

## Schooling Has Exploded

::: incremental
- 1950: average adult in low-income countries had ~2 years of schooling
- 2020: average adult has ~7 years
- Primary enrollment in sub-Saharan Africa: 52% in 1970, 98% by 2015
- Gains are largest among girls and in the poorest countries
:::

## But Learning Has Not

::: incremental
- More years in school do not automatically mean more learning
- In rural India, ~50% of grade 5 students cannot read a grade 2 text
- In many low-income countries, grade 3 students cannot do single-digit subtraction
- The "learning crisis": enrollment up, skills flat
:::

## Why Might Education Pay?

::: incremental
- **Human capital (Becker)**: school builds productive skills; higher skill → higher wages
- **Signaling (Spence, 1973)**: school reveals underlying ability to employers
- Both predict: more school → higher wages
- They disagree on *why*, and on what policy should do
:::

## Becker: Skills

::: incremental
- Workers choose schooling like an investment
- Costs: tuition, forgone earnings
- Returns: higher productivity, higher wages over lifetime
- Implication: expanding schools should raise wages, because new skills are being built
:::

## Spence: Signals

::: incremental
- Ability is unobservable to employers at hiring
- High-ability workers find school cheap; low-ability workers find it costly
- A diploma separates types even if the content is useless
- Implication: expanding schools may not raise wages if it only shifts the signal
:::

## Why the Distinction Matters

::: incremental
- Human capital: policy should build more schools, train more teachers
- Signaling: policy should fund only the credential, or find cheaper signals
- Most evidence suggests both are at play; pure signaling is rare
- Testing them requires variation that breaks the ability-schooling link
:::

# The Causal Problem

## OLS Returns to Schooling

$$\ln(\text{wage}_i) = \alpha + \beta \cdot \text{school}_i + \varepsilon_i$$

::: incremental
- Typical OLS estimate: $\hat\beta \approx 0.08$ to $0.10$
- Interpretation: one more year of school is associated with 8-10% higher wages
- "Associated with", not "causes"
:::

## Ability Bias

::: incremental
- High-ability people get more schooling AND earn more
- OLS attributes the full wage gap to schooling
- True causal effect is smaller than the correlation
- Classic upward bias
:::

## Reverse Causation and Selection

::: incremental
- Richer families can afford more schooling; their kids also inherit networks, health, nutrition
- Poor regions have worse schools AND worse labor markets
- Any observed correlation mixes all of these
- We need exogenous variation in schooling
:::

## Classic Fixes

::: incremental
- **Twins studies**: compare siblings to hold genes constant
- **Compulsory schooling laws**: use legal cutoffs as a shock
- Both mostly come from rich countries
- Do they apply in low-income settings where access, not motivation, is the bind?
:::

# Difference-in-Differences

## The Setup

::: incremental
- Some units get treated; others do not
- We observe outcomes before and after
- Simple comparison of treated post-treatment is confounded by unit differences
- Simple before-after on treated is confounded by time trends
:::

## The 2×2 Table

|            | Before | After |
|------------|--------|-------|
| Treated    | $Y_{T,0}$ | $Y_{T,1}$ |
| Control    | $Y_{C,0}$ | $Y_{C,1}$ |

. . .

$$\hat\delta_{DiD} = (Y_{T,1} - Y_{T,0}) - (Y_{C,1} - Y_{C,0})$$

## What DiD Assumes

::: incremental
- **Parallel trends**: without treatment, treated and control would have evolved the same way
- Unit fixed effects absorb any time-invariant differences
- Time fixed effects absorb any common shocks
- The treatment effect lives in the interaction
:::

## DiD as a Regression

$$Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \delta (\text{Treated}_i \times \text{Post}_t) + \varepsilon_{it}$$

::: incremental
- $\alpha_i$: unit fixed effects (absorbs level differences)
- $\lambda_t$: time fixed effects (absorbs common trends)
- $\delta$: coefficient on the interaction = DiD estimate
- DiD is an interaction term, nothing more
:::

## Why This Matters Today

::: incremental
- Duflo (2001) uses a continuous DiD: intensity of treatment × exposure cohort
- The interaction of *how much* treatment and *who was exposed* is the instrument
- Same logic, more variation
:::

# Duflo (2001)

## The Setting

::: incremental
- Indonesia, early 1970s: primary enrollment ~60%, large regional gaps
- 1973 oil windfall funds a massive public investment
- 1973-1978: INPRES program builds 61,807 primary schools
- Roughly doubles the existing stock in five years
:::

## The Allocation Rule

::: incremental
- Schools allocated across 283 regions
- Rule: more schools to regions with *fewer* existing schools per child
- Program intensity = schools built per 1,000 children in region
- Not random, but driven by a formula, not local demand
:::

## Two Dimensions of Variation

::: incremental
- **Region**: some regions got more schools (high intensity)
- **Cohort**: some children were young enough to benefit, others had already finished primary school
- Children aged 2-6 in 1974: fully exposed
- Children aged 12+ in 1974: already past primary
:::

## The Design

::: incremental
- High-intensity region + young cohort = most treatment
- Low-intensity region + old cohort = no treatment
- Compare the difference across cohorts in high vs low-intensity regions
- Continuous DiD: intensity × exposure
:::

## The Identifying Assumption

::: incremental
- Without INPRES, young cohorts in high-intensity regions would have evolved like young cohorts in low-intensity regions
- Threat: maybe high-intensity regions were catching up for other reasons
- Test: look at cohorts *too old* to be treated
- If their education rises with intensity, parallel trends fails
:::

## Placebo Cohorts

::: incremental
- Compare ages 12-17 vs ages 18-24 in 1974
- Neither group was exposed to INPRES schools
- If intensity predicts differences between these cohorts, we have a problem
- It does not; the effect turns on precisely at age 12
:::

## First Stage: Education

::: incremental
- One more school per 1,000 children → 0.12 to 0.19 more years of schooling
- Effect concentrated at primary completion, not secondary
- Larger in sparser, poorer regions (where the constraint was bindings)
- Consistent with supply-side access story
:::

## Reduced Form: Wages

::: incremental
- One more school per 1,000 children → 1.5% to 2.7% higher adult wages
- Same cohort × intensity interaction, now on earnings
- Estimated in 1995, ~20 years after exposure
:::

## From DiD to IV

::: incremental
- First stage: intensity × exposure → more schooling
- Reduced form: intensity × exposure → higher wages
- Ratio: wage effect per year of schooling
- This is 2SLS: the interaction is an instrument for education
:::

## 2SLS Returns

::: incremental
- Returns to education: **6.8% to 10.6%** per year
- OLS returns in the same data: ~7.5%
- In this setting, OLS is not wildly biased
- But the IV estimate is a LATE, not an average
:::

## LATE Interpretation

::: incremental
- 2SLS identifies the return for **compliers**: students induced to attend by the new schools
- These are children who would not have gone without INPRES
- Likely poorer, more rural, more credit-constrained
- Their return need not equal the return for infra-marginal students
:::

## Cost-Benefit

::: incremental
- Cost per school: ~$24,300 in 1990 USD
- Implied internal rate of return: 8.8% to 12%
- Competitive with returns to physical capital
- Supply-side education investment paid for itself
:::

## What to Take Away

::: incremental
- Access, not just demand, was a real constraint in 1970s Indonesia
- A continuous DiD with an interaction instrument isolates causal returns
- Returns to schooling are positive and economically meaningful
- Human capital story wins here; pure signaling cannot explain wage gains from *building more schools*
:::

## Limitations

::: incremental
- LATE: results apply to compliers, not everyone
- Indonesia in 1995: formal-sector wages, not informal or agricultural
- Primary schooling, not secondary or tertiary
- Learning crisis literature suggests building schools today may not pay the same return
:::

# Wrapping Up

## What Education Economics Teaches

::: incremental
- Education correlates with development, but correlation is not causation
- Credible designs turn on variation that breaks the ability-schooling link
- Duflo (2001): supply-side shocks + DiD + IV = a clean answer
- The learning crisis is the open frontier: years of school are rising; skills are not
:::
